opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to separate two phases, because the answer is pretty different depending on where you are in the transition.

In the early and middle phases, when AI automates some tasks but not others, the story can actually be fairly good for workers. AI makes the economy much more productive, and the tasks that are still bottlenecked on human labor become more valuable. That's the standard story with complementary inputs. If AI handles a big chunk of what a job involves, the remaining human parts become the scarce input, and wages for those parts can go up. So for a while I'd expect a lot of people to see rising wages, even as the composition of what they do changes quite dramatically.

The problem comes as you approach full automation. Once AI systems and robots can do essentially everything a human worker can do, at lower cost, the wage a human can command is capped by what it costs to run the machine that does the same job. If that cost keeps falling, and I expect it would, then human wages in competitive markets eventually fall too, potentially below what people need to live on. Labor stops being a scarce factor of production. So the long-run picture for labor *income* specifically is not great.

But I'd emphasize that this isn't the same as saying people will be worse off. The economy in that world would be enormously larger. Output could grow far faster than anything we've seen historically. The question becomes one of distribution: who owns the capital, the compute, the land, the AI systems themselves? If the gains flow through ownership, then people who hold assets do extremely well, and people who rely only on wages are in a precarious position unless there's some kind of redistribution.

So my honest view is that the main challenge isn't really "will there be enough wealth," it's whether our institutions adapt so that people who no longer have valuable labor to sell still have a claim on that wealth. That could be broad asset ownership, sovereign wealth funds, taxation and transfers, something like that. Historically, workers have had bargaining power partly because their labor was needed. In a fully automated economy that leverage goes away, and I think that's the political economy question people should be thinking about much more seriously than whether some particular job survives the next five years.

r001.rationale: The response says productivity may make the economy much larger, but it does not use that to predict wages will stay at or above their previous level under full automation; it says wages may fall below what people need to live on.

r002.rationale: It predicts wages for remaining human tasks may rise during partial automation, but does not say employed workers will earn substantially higher real wages.

r003.rationale: It describes remaining human tasks becoming more valuable and jobs changing, but does not explain that workers can move from automated tasks to tasks not yet automated to limit unemployment.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss retraining or the risk that a new occupation could be automated before retraining pays off.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on where you are in the process, and people tend to conflate two very different phases.

In the early and middle stages, where AI is automating some tasks but not others, I actually expect workers to do reasonably well on average. The reason is that when you automate part of the economy, the parts that aren't automated become the bottleneck, and the people doing those tasks capture a lot of the gains. This is basically what happened throughout the Industrial Revolution and the twentieth century. Wages rose enormously even though an enormous fraction of the jobs that existed in 1800 were automated away. The complementary tasks became more valuable, and the labor share of income stayed roughly stable for a very long time.

So I don't think the transition period is the scary part for wages in aggregate. There will be distributional effects, some occupations will get hit hard and others won't, and that reshuffling can be painful for specific people. But the median worker probably sees rising wages during a period where AI is a strong complement to human labor rather than a full substitute.

The part that worries me more is the end state. Once AI systems can do essentially everything a human can do, and crucially can do it more cheaply, then the economic logic changes. Human labor stops being a bottleneck on anything. At that point the wage of a human worker gets pinned to whatever it costs to run an AI doing the same job, and that cost is probably falling rapidly. In a world with full automation, wages could decline quite substantially even as total output is exploding, because the thing that's scarce is no longer labor. It's capital, compute, energy, land, whatever the actual physical constraints are.

So you get this strange picture where the economy might be growing at twenty or thirty percent a year, and yet the returns to being a human who can work are collapsing. The gains go to whoever owns the capital. That's not a world where people starve, necessarily, because the economy is so much larger that redistribution is cheap in relative terms. But it does mean that labor income, which is how most people have historically gotten their share of economic output, stops being a reliable mechanism.

Which is why I think the political question matters more than the economic one in the long run. If you own a slice of the capital, or if there's some institutional arrangement that gives people a claim on output that doesn't depend on their labor, you're fine, in fact you're vastly better off than anyone today. If neither of those is true, you're in a precarious position regardless of how large the economy gets. I don't think we have great answers to that yet, and I'd rather people start thinking about it now while labor still has bargaining power than wait until it doesn't.

r001.rationale: The response says full automation could cause human wages to decline as labor ceases to be a bottleneck; it does not identify productivity gains as a reason wages might stay above their previous level.

r002.rationale: It predicts rising wages for the median worker during partial automation, but does not clearly predict substantially higher real wages for workers who remain employed.

r003.rationale: It says nonautomated tasks become more valuable, but does not explain that workers can move into those tasks to limit unemployment.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss retraining or the risk that a new occupation may be automated before retraining pays off.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish the transition from what happens once you actually have full automation. During the transition, AI could make many workers more productive, and that can raise their wages. But it can also substitute for particular kinds of labor, so there’s no guarantee that everyone benefits, or that the adjustment is smooth.

If you really mean full automation—machines can do everything a human worker can do, at a lower cost—then labor stops being a scarce input into production. At that point, I wouldn’t expect wages to remain the main way people receive income. You can have an enormously wealthy economy in which people’s ability to earn money by working has fallen dramatically.

So the question becomes: who owns the capital, and how is the income from that capital distributed? People could fare very well if they have ownership stakes or receive some share of the output through public policy. But greater productive capacity doesn’t, by itself, ensure that outcome. I’m optimistic about the potential for higher living standards; I think the distribution of those gains is a separate question that we have to take seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says productivity gains during the transition could raise wages, but does not identify that as a reason wages might avoid falling below their previous level under full automation.

r002.rationale: It says AI could raise wages for many workers, but does not predict substantially higher real wages for workers who remain employed during partial automation.

r003.rationale: The response does not explain that workers may move from automated tasks to tasks that are not yet automated.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss retraining or how the pace of automation could make retraining a poor investment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on the stage of automation we’re talking about. While AI can do some tasks but still needs people to do others, workers can benefit quite substantially. If the tasks you do become a bottleneck, automating the things around you can make your labor more valuable. So I wouldn’t expect every improvement in AI to translate into lower wages or fewer jobs.

But as you approach full automation, that argument becomes much weaker. If a machine can do essentially everything you can do, and we can produce more of those machines cheaply, it’s hard to see why your labor would continue to command a high wage. There might still be demand for human interaction or for things specifically made by humans, but that’s a different proposition from saying everyone will have an economically valuable job.

The important distinction is between what happens to wages and what happens to living standards. Full automation could make society enormously richer while reducing the share of income people receive from working. Whether workers benefit in that world depends on whether they have access to that wealth through ownership, transfers, or some other arrangement. So I’m optimistic about the productive potential, but I don’t think a good outcome for workers follows automatically from that.

r001.rationale: The response says full automation could make society richer while reducing workers’ share of income; it does not claim productivity gains would keep wages from falling below their previous level.

r002.rationale: It says workers may benefit and their labor may become more valuable during partial automation, but does not predict substantially higher real wages for those who remain employed.

r003.rationale: It describes automating surrounding tasks as potentially increasing a worker’s value, but does not explain that moving to tasks not yet automated can limit unemployment.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss retraining or whether rapid automation makes retraining a poor investment.
